title: Foraging dandelion leaves and flowers
subtitle: Year-round harvest, best season, and bitter reduction
excerpt: Dandelion grows in most UK lawns, verges, and field margins year-round. Young spring leaves are the least bitter and most useful. The flowers make a simple cordial. This guide covers picking, bitter reduction, and the few plants to distinguish from.
sourceNotes: Richard Mabey, Food for Free (1972); John Wright, The Forager's Calendar (2019); BSBI species accounts for Taraxacum officinale; Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

glossaryTerms.definition: Matching three independent visual, scent, or habitat features before eating any wild plant. All three must match; a single mismatch means stop.
A wild plant that resembles an edible species closely enough to cause misidentification. Many look-alikes are toxic.

content.text: Dandelion (Taraxacum officinale) grows in most UK lawns, roadside verges, field margins, and waste ground throughout the year. Young spring leaves from March to May are the least bitter and the best choice for eating raw in salads. The bright yellow flower heads open from March onward and can be used in cordials and fritters. Verify your identification before eating; if in doubt, do not eat.
Apply the
rule-of-three identification

: confirm (1) the deeply lobed leaves arranged in a flat rosette at ground level, (2) the single hollow stem with milky white sap when broken, and (3) the single bright yellow composite flower head. All three must match.
ID features
Leaves: deeply lobed, the teeth pointing backward toward the base like a row of lions' teeth. Arranged flat in a rosette from a central tap root.
Stem: single, hollow, leafless, producing milky white sap when broken. Grows 5 to 30 cm depending on conditions.
Flower head: a single round head of many bright yellow ray florets. Turns to a familiar round seed clock when finished.
Poisonous look-alikes
Several UK plants with yellow daisy-like flowers are mistaken for dandelion; most are not toxic but some cause digestive upset. The main
look-alike plants
to distinguish:
Cat's ear (Hypochaeris radicata): similar rosette and yellow flower. The stem is branched and solid, not hollow. Leaves have rounded lobes rather than pointed ones.
Celandine (Ranunculus ficaria): yellow flower in early spring, but the leaves are heart-shaped and glossy, not lobed, and the stem produces no milky sap. Toxic if eaten in quantity.
When and how to harvest

Pick young leaves in March and April for the least bitterness. From May onward the leaves are larger and more bitter; blanching in boiling water for 30 seconds and draining reduces the bitterness before using in cooked dishes. Pick flowers in full sun when they are fully open; they close on cold or cloudy days.
Avoid picking from roadsides, recently sprayed verges, or dog-walked areas. Pick from your own garden or from unsprayed grassland you know.
After harvesting

Rinse leaves in cold water. Use the same day if possible; they wilt and become more bitter within 24 hours. Young leaves go raw into salads with a vinaigrette. Flowers can be scattered on salads, battered and fried as fritters, or steeped in hot water with lemon and sugar for a simple cordial.
Legal and ethical

The Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and Theft Act 1968 allow collection of foliage and flowers from common land and verges for personal use. Private land requires the landowner's permission. Dandelion is common and abundant; there is no conservation concern with moderate harvest.

rows.symptom: Leaves are very bitter even in spring
rows.cause: Picking large mature leaves rather than small young ones, or picking in summer rather than spring
rows.fix: Select the smallest leaves in the centre of the rosette. If the leaves are large and dark green, blanch briefly to reduce bitterness before using.

rows.symptom: Stem does not produce milky sap when broken
rows.cause: The plant may be cat's ear or another non-dandelion species with a solid stem
rows.fix: Confirm the hollow stem with milky sap as part of the rule-of-three check. Solid stems mean a different plant.
